S027.name: Sleep_Disturbance
S027.description: A state where there is a significant change in the quantity or quality of sleep.

subtypes.Initial Insomnia: Difficulty falling asleep and taking a long time to do so.
subtypes.Middle Insomnia: Waking up frequently during sleep or having difficulty falling back asleep.
subtypes.Early Morning Awakening: Waking up too early and being unable to fall back asleep.
subtypes.Hypersomnia: Sleeping for long periods at night or excessive sleep during the day.
subtypes.Nightmare Disorder: Sleep disturbance caused by repeated and distressing dreams.
subtypes.Non-Restorative Sleep: Feeling unrefreshed despite having slept enough.

S069.name: Intrusive_Symptoms
S069.description: Recurrent, involuntary, and intrusive distressing memories of the traumatic event.

subtypes.Intrusive Memories: Recurrent, involuntary, and intrusive distressing memories of the traumatic event.
subtypes.Distressing Dreams: Recurrent distressing dreams in which the content and/or affect of the dream are related to the traumatic event.
subtypes.Dissociative Reactions (Flashbacks): Dissociative reactions (e.g., flashbacks) in which the individual feels or acts as if the traumatic event were recurring.
subtypes.Psychological Distress at Cues: Intense or prolonged psychological distress at exposure to internal or external cues that symbolize or resemble an aspect of the traumatic event.
subtypes.Physiological Reactions to Cues: Marked physiological reactions to internal or external cues that symbolize or resemble an aspect of the traumatic event.

S071.name: Trauma_Related_Amnesia
S071.description: Inability to remember an important aspect of the traumatic event (typically due to dissociative amnesia and not to other factors like head injury or alcohol).

subtypes.Fragmented Memory: Inability to recall only specific parts of the traumatic event while remembering others.
subtypes.Generalized Amnesia: Inability to recall the majority or the entirety of the traumatic event.

S076.name: Inability_Positive_Emotions
S076.description: Persistent inability to experience positive emotions (e.g., inability to experience happiness, satisfaction, or loving feelings).

subtypes.Anhedonia for Happiness: Unable to feel happiness or joy even when good things happen.
subtypes.Lack of Satisfaction: Unable to experience satisfaction or pride even after achieving something good.
subtypes.Inability to Feel Love: Feeling numb to love or affection towards family or lovers.
subtypes.Emotional Numbness: A state where the mind feels empty and nothing is felt, as if all positive emotions are blocked.

S077.name: Irritability_Aggression
S077.description: Irritable behavior and angry outbursts (with little or no provocation) typically expressed as verbal or physical aggression.

subtypes.Impulsive Anger: Sudden explosions of anger for trivial reasons or no clear reason.
subtypes.Verbal Aggression: Attacking others with shouting, cursing, or blame without holding back.
subtypes.Physical Aggression: Physically attacking people or throwing/breaking objects.
subtypes.Chronic Irritability: A state where nerves are always sharp and sensitive, ready to explode at the slightest touch.

S079.name: Hypervigilance
S079.description: Persistent state of being alert and tense about the surrounding environment.

subtypes.Scanning for Danger: Always scanning the surroundings and being alert to find potential threats or risks.
subtypes.Safety Checking: Repetitively confirming safety, such as checking exit locations or observing people around.
subtypes.Sustained Alertness: Unable to relax tension even in safe environments and maintaining a constant state of alertness.

symptom.disease_info: Acute Stress Disorder (ASD) is characterized by the development of anxiety, dissociative, and other stress-related symptoms within three days to one month following exposure to a traumatic event involving actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violation. Core clinical features include intrusive recollections, avoidance, negative mood, dissociation, and marked arousal, with associated functional impairment. Symptoms must arise shortly after the trauma and resolve within a month; persistence beyond this period suggests possible progression to Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD). ASD is distinguished from normative stress reactions by its severity, breadth of symptoms, and degree of interference with daily functioning, and from PTSD primarily by its shorter duration and greater emphasis on dissociative phenomena.

patient.personality: Carl is a quietly disciplined, methodical retiree with a competitive chess player’s mind, a meticulous approach to woodworking, and a thoughtful curiosity about art and history.
patient.stressor: Carl was out in his backyard workshop one afternoon, working alone on a large piece of oak, when a table saw kickback threw the board and dragged his hand dangerously close to the spinning blade, leaving a deep gash and narrowly missing several fingers. He managed to wrap his hand and drive himself to the emergency room, where staff told him that if the board had shifted a fraction of an inch more, he could have lost most of his hand; the combination of sudden blood loss, the noise of the saw, and the vivid explanations of potential damage left him shaken. In the weeks that followed, he tried to resume his orderly retirement routines—chess at the community center, tending his garden, and teaching basic woodworking—but each attempt to return to the workshop or even handle certain tools left him unsettled and unable to settle into his usual evening rest, with his nights becoming increasingly disrupted and leaving him tired and less engaged in his normal activities. After about three weeks of poor sleep and mounting frustration that he could no longer enjoy his woodworking or focus on reading and painting because he felt so worn down, his wife and adult daughter encouraged him to see a psychiatrist to understand why this one incident was still affecting him so strongly.
patient.chief_complaint: “Since that accident with the saw, my sleep has been completely off—I just can’t seem to get a full, restful night anymore.”

S027.name: Sleep_Disturbance
S027.description: A state where there is a significant change in the quantity or quality of sleep.
S027.manifestation: Most nights I lie there for an hour or more replaying the day and that accident before I can fall asleep, and then I jerk awake two or three times with my heart pounding like the saw just kicked back again, so I wake up feeling like I never really slept at all.

S069.name: Intrusive_Symptoms
S069.description: Recurrent, involuntary, and intrusive distressing memories of the traumatic event.
S069.manifestation: Out of nowhere, even when I’m just sitting at the chess club or reading, I suddenly see that board flying back at me and my hand hanging over the blade, and for a few seconds it’s so vivid I can almost hear the saw whining and feel the blood running again.

S071.name: Trauma_Related_Amnesia
S071.description: Inability to remember an important aspect of the traumatic event (typically due to dissociative amnesia and not to other factors like head injury or alcohol).
S071.manifestation: What bothers me is that there are blank spots when I try to think about the actual moment it happened—I can remember setting up the cut and then being in the car driving to the ER, but the instant the board kicked and exactly how my hand got sliced is just missing, like a skipped page in a book.

S076.name: Inability_Positive_Emotions
S076.description: Persistent inability to experience positive emotions (e.g., inability to experience happiness, satisfaction, or loving feelings).
S076.manifestation: Even when my granddaughter comes over or I finish a good chess game online, I just feel flat, like I’m watching myself go through the motions instead of actually feeling pleased or proud the way I used to.

S077.name: Irritability_Aggression
S077.description: Irritable behavior and angry outbursts (with little or no provocation) typically expressed as verbal or physical aggression.
S077.manifestation: I’ve noticed I snap at my wife over little things, like her asking how my hand is or suggesting we watch a movie, and I hear my voice coming out sharp and annoyed even though I know she’s just trying to help.

S079.name: Hypervigilance
S079.description: Persistent state of being alert and tense about the surrounding environment.
S079.manifestation: Since the accident I catch myself constantly listening for noises, checking where my hands are, and scanning the room—especially around tools or loud sounds—so even sitting in my own living room I feel keyed up, like I’m waiting for something else to go wrong.
